fixes.answer: Absolutely, I am a firm believer in lifelong learning. The idea that education ends when you leave school is completely [[outdated]], especially in today's fast-changing world. Continuing to learn [[keeps the mind sharp]], opens new opportunities and helps people adapt to change. Beyond practical benefits, I think curiosity and growth are essential to a fulfilling life. Learning should be a [[lifelong pursuit]], not a phase.
fixes.why: 4 marks with plain 'phase'; merged 'lifelong pursuit' and marked 'outdated' and 'keeps the mind sharp'

fixes.answer: There are [[trade-offs]] at each stage. Young people generally absorb new information, especially languages, more easily, and have fewer competing responsibilities. However, adult learners bring focus, motivation and real-world experience that can make their learning more [[purposeful]] and efficient. So while children may have a biological advantage, adults [[compensate]] with discipline and context. Neither is simply easier; it depends on what is being learned.

It is primarily because of the [[breakneck pace]] of technological change. Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become [[obsolete]], and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and [[reskill]]. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. In short, adaptability through learning has become a genuine necessity, not a luxury.

A society that embraces lifelong learning tends to be more adaptable, innovative and [[economically resilient]], as its workforce can respond to change. It also promotes [[social mobility]], giving people second chances to improve their prospects. On a personal level, continued learning keeps older people mentally active and engaged, which benefits public health. So it strengthens both the economy and the overall [[vitality]] of a community.
fixes.why: 'engaged' and 'economy' are plain; marked 'economically resilient' and 'social mobility'

fixes.answer: I am confident it will, [[out of sheer necessity]]. As careers become less linear and technology evolves ever faster, continuous learning and periodic reskilling will simply be part of working life. I anticipate more flexible, [[bite-sized]] courses and employer-sponsored training becoming [[commonplace]]. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.
fixes.why: 'ongoing' and 'process' are plain; marked 'out of sheer necessity' and 'bite-sized'

fixes.answer: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. To address this, flexible online and part-time courses are invaluable, as is employer support through funded training. Governments could also offer [[subsidies]] or learning accounts. [[Dismantling]] these obstacles would make lifelong learning genuinely [[attainable]] for everyone.

There can be. While staying current is beneficial, the constant pressure to reskill can be exhausting and stressful, creating a feeling that you can never [[rest on your achievements]]. It may also breed anxiety about becoming obsolete. For some, particularly older workers, this [[relentless]] demand can feel genuinely overwhelming. So although the principle is sound, the pace of change can make it feel like a [[burden]] rather than a joy.
fixes.why: 'obsolete' repeated from Q3 and 'overwhelming' plain; marked 'rest on your achievements' and 'relentless'
